ai-evaluation.shortDefinition: AI evaluation is the systematic practice of testing whether an AI application is fit for a defined real-world use, including model behavior, adversarial failure modes, user interaction, and downstream outcomes.
ai-evaluation.fullDefinition: AI evaluation begins by defining the application, intended users, context, success criteria, and consequential failures. It then gathers evidence at multiple levels rather than relying on a single benchmark. Model testing examines technical behavior under controlled conditions; red teaming deliberately probes weaknesses and misuse; user testing examines how people actually interact with and are affected by the system. Verification and validation ask whether the system was built as intended and whether it is suitable for its real purpose. Evaluation should continue after deployment because models, prompts, tools, data, users, and operating conditions change.
ai-evaluation.whyItMatters: A strong benchmark score does not establish that an AI application will work safely or effectively in its deployment context. NIST's 2026 ARIA Evaluation Planning Manual describes holistic AI evaluation as combining model testing, red teaming, and user testing, while the 2026 TEVV-Athlon draft emphasizes evaluation that is adaptable to the application and attentive to real-world impacts and outcomes.
realWorldScenarios: A support team first measures answer quality on a representative test set, then probes prompt-injection and policy failures, and finally observes whether real agents can recognize and correct weak suggestions.
A research assistant is evaluated separately for retrieval quality, citation correctness, synthesis quality, and the user's ability to notice unsupported claims.
An agentic workflow is tested when tools fail, permissions are missing, instructions conflict, or an action would be difficult to reverse.
beginnerActions: Write down the intended user, task, context, and consequence of failure before choosing a metric.
Create a representative evaluation set with ordinary cases, edge cases, and known failure examples.
Compare the AI workflow with a meaningful baseline instead of judging impressive examples in isolation.
intermediateActions: Separate model testing, adversarial or red-team testing, and user testing so each answers a different question.
Measure dimensions such as factuality, task success, safety, latency, cost, and recoverability only where they matter to the use case.
Classify failures by source—model, prompt, retrieval, tool, data, interface, policy, or human interaction—so fixes target the right layer.
advancedActions: Build repeatable regression evaluations that run when models, prompts, retrieval, tools, policies, or interfaces change.
Design risk-based test coverage that gives high-consequence and hard-to-reverse failures deeper scrutiny.
Combine production monitoring with user feedback and incident evidence, then feed representative failures back into evaluation suites.
commonMistakes: Treating a public benchmark as proof of fitness for a specific application.
Testing only model outputs while ignoring how people use, misunderstand, override, or depend on them.
Calling ordinary test cases red teaming without deliberately probing adversarial or stress conditions.
Using the same model to generate and unquestioningly grade its own answers.
Optimizing one aggregate score while hiding severe failure categories.
Changing models or prompts without regression testing.
ai-evaluation.evidenceSummary: NIST's September 2026 ARIA Evaluation Planning Manual describes holistic application evaluation using three complementary forms of evidence: model testing, red teaming, and user testing. NIST's August 2026 TEVV-Athlon initial public draft presents an extensible framework for testing, evaluation, verification, and validation that can be customized across AI applications and focuses on real-world impacts and outcomes.
scholarlyNotes: NIST (2026), ARIA Evaluation Planning Manual: Elements of ARIA-Style AI Evaluations, NIST AI 200-3. https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.200-3
NIST (2026), The TEVV-Athlon Framework for Evaluating AI Systems, initial public draft. https://www.nist.gov/artificial-intelligence/ai-research/tevv-athlon-framework-evaluating-ai-systems
NIST (2025), Assessing Risks and Impacts of AI (ARIA): Pilot Evaluation Report, NIST AI 700-2. https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.700-2
ai-evaluation.howToMeasureProgress: A mature evaluator can explain what each test establishes, what it does not establish, which failures matter most, how users affect system performance, and whether evidence represents the deployment context. Progress is visible when evaluations reliably detect regressions and change deployment decisions—not when the test suite merely becomes larger.
ai-evaluation.aiEraRelevance: As models become easier to swap and capabilities change quickly, durable advantage shifts from memorizing one model's behavior to building evaluation systems that reveal whether a new model, prompt, agent, or workflow actually improves outcomes without introducing unacceptable failure modes.

fact-checking.shortDefinition: Fact-checking is the disciplined process of turning a checkable claim into an evidence question, locating the best available sources, testing context and provenance, and reporting what the evidence does and does not establish.
fact-checking.fullDefinition: Fact-checking is narrower and more rigorous than general skepticism. It begins by isolating a specific factual claim, identifying what evidence could confirm or contradict it, prioritizing primary and authoritative sources, tracing quotations and statistics to origin, checking dates and definitions, and distinguishing direct evidence from inference. Good fact-checking also preserves uncertainty when evidence is incomplete or genuinely contested.
fact-checking.whyItMatters: Generative AI and high-speed publishing make plausible but unsupported claims inexpensive to produce. Reliable verification therefore depends on provenance and evidence rather than fluency, repetition, or search visibility.
realWorldScenarios: An editor traces a viral statistic through several articles until finding the underlying dataset and discovers that the quoted population differs from the article's claim.
A researcher opens an AI-supplied citation and checks whether the paper actually supports the sentence attached to it.
A marketer verifies a competitor comparison against current first-party documentation before publishing it.
beginnerActions: Rewrite a broad statement as one specific claim that could be checked.
Locate the original source behind one statistic or quotation.
Record the date, population, definition, and relevant context for quantitative evidence.
intermediateActions: Use independent evidence rather than counting multiple articles that all repeat the same source.
Check whether a source supports the exact claim rather than merely discussing the same topic.
Label conclusions as confirmed, contradicted, uncertain, or unsupported according to the evidence instead of forcing a binary verdict.
advancedActions: Build editorial claim-review workflows that preserve source provenance from draft through publication.
Develop verification depth proportional to the consequence and reversibility of an error.
Audit published material periodically when claims depend on changing data, policies, prices, standards, or technology.
commonMistakes: Treating repeated claims as independent confirmation.
Using a citation whose title sounds relevant without reading the source.
Ignoring the population or time period behind a statistic.
Replacing evidence with an AI confidence statement.
Overstating certainty when credible evidence remains incomplete.
fact-checking.howToMeasureProgress: Track how often published claims can be traced to suitable evidence, how many verification checks catch errors before publication, whether corrections become less frequent for repeated error types, and whether uncertainty is represented accurately.
fact-checking.aiEraRelevance: AI can accelerate source discovery and comparison, but it can also fabricate citations or confidently misstate sources. Fact-checking becomes the control layer that separates generated plausibility from evidence-backed publication.

digital-accessibility.shortDefinition: Digital accessibility is the practice of designing and maintaining digital content and interfaces so people with diverse disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate, and operate them.
digital-accessibility.fullDefinition: Accessibility is a product and content quality discipline, not a final compliance pass. It includes semantic structure, keyboard access, focus behavior, text alternatives, captions, readable contrast, understandable language, error identification, adaptable layouts, and compatibility with assistive technologies. Effective accessibility work combines standards with testing because technical conformance alone does not guarantee a usable experience.
digital-accessibility.whyItMatters: Digital services increasingly mediate education, employment, commerce, and public participation. Accessibility reduces barriers for people with visual, auditory, motor, cognitive, speech, and other disabilities and often improves clarity and robustness for a wider audience.
realWorldScenarios: A developer verifies that a form can be completed using only a keyboard and that errors are programmatically associated with the relevant fields.
A content creator writes useful alternative text based on an image's purpose instead of mechanically describing every visible detail.
A design team includes accessibility checks in component development so the same defect is not reproduced across dozens of pages.
beginnerActions: Navigate one important page using only the keyboard and document blockers.
Check heading structure, form labels, link purpose, image alternatives, and captions on representative content.
Use automated accessibility tools as a first pass, then manually inspect issues they cannot determine.
intermediateActions: Test common flows with screen-reader and keyboard workflows rather than checking isolated components only.
Build accessible states for errors, loading, focus, modals, menus, and dynamic updates.
Add accessibility acceptance criteria to design and engineering work before implementation.
advancedActions: Create reusable accessible components and regression tests that prevent recurring defects.
Include disabled users or qualified accessibility testers in research for high-value journeys.
Track accessibility defects by severity, recurrence, component, and user impact so systemic issues are fixed at their source.
commonMistakes: Assuming automated scanners can prove a site is accessible.
Adding ARIA attributes where native semantic HTML already provides the correct behavior.
Treating accessibility as a launch-day checklist.
Using placeholder text as a form label.
Assuming an AI-generated interface is accessible because it looks visually clean.
digital-accessibility.howToMeasureProgress: Measure completion of important tasks with keyboard and assistive-technology workflows, severity and recurrence of defects, accessibility of shared components, and how early accessibility issues are caught in the product lifecycle.
digital-accessibility.aiEraRelevance: AI can help draft alternative text, code, captions, and audits, but generated output still requires contextual review and user testing. Accessibility is a strong example of why automated checks and human experience must complement each other.

source-synthesis.shortDefinition: Source synthesis is the ability to combine evidence from multiple sources into a coherent account that preserves agreements, disagreements, scope, provenance, and uncertainty.
source-synthesis.fullDefinition: Synthesis is not a stack of summaries. It organizes sources around questions, claims, methods, or themes and compares what each source actually contributes. Strong synthesis notices when sources use different definitions or populations, distinguishes independent evidence from repeated reporting, explains meaningful disagreement, and builds a conclusion no broader than the combined evidence allows.
source-synthesis.whyItMatters: Modern research often produces more information than a reader can inspect directly. Search and generative AI can compress that information quickly, but compression can erase methodological differences, uncertainty, and source lineage unless synthesis is performed deliberately.
realWorldScenarios: A writer compares several labour-market reports and separates findings about different countries rather than blending them into one universal claim.
A product researcher combines interviews, support tickets, and usage data while explaining what each evidence type can and cannot establish.
An analyst discovers that five articles making the same claim all depend on one press release and treats them as one evidence lineage rather than five confirmations.
beginnerActions: Create a source matrix with claims, evidence, population or context, date, and limitations.
Group research by question or theme rather than writing one paragraph per source.
Mark which claims are directly supported and which are your inference.
intermediateActions: Reconcile differences in definitions, measurement, populations, and time periods before combining findings.
Identify shared source lineage so repeated reporting is not mistaken for independent corroboration.
Represent meaningful disagreement explicitly and explain what evidence would help resolve it.
advancedActions: Develop synthesis workflows that preserve claim-level provenance from notes into publication.
Weight evidence according to relevance and methodological strength rather than prestige or volume alone.
Produce conclusions that remain useful while making uncertainty and scope visible to decision-makers.
commonMistakes: Writing sequential summaries instead of integrating evidence.
Combining incompatible statistics because they use similar labels.
Counting syndicated or derivative reporting as independent evidence.
Flattening legitimate disagreement into a false consensus.
Letting AI produce a polished synthesis without checking whether it distorted the underlying sources.
source-synthesis.howToMeasureProgress: A strong synthesis lets a reader trace important conclusions to evidence, understand why sources agree or disagree, see the limits of generalization, and distinguish independent evidence from repetition. Measure clarity and traceability rather than the number of sources cited.
source-synthesis.aiEraRelevance: AI is exceptionally fast at summarization but can flatten distinctions among sources. Source synthesis is therefore a high-value human skill for supervising generated research and turning large evidence sets into trustworthy conclusions.
